description: Checked-in content corrections applied at build time to normalized Notion content, keyed by Notion blockId and guarded by the block's original text. Each entry is also published on /errata/. If a guard stops matching (for example because the fix was made in Notion and re-pulled), the build fails: retire or update the entry.

entries.summary: For the move 'add 1 to two chosen elements', the note claimed every fixed pairwise difference is unchanged. Only the chosen pair's difference is preserved; the invariant is the parity of the sum, and matching parity is necessary but not sufficient.
entries.original: Invariant: The difference a_i - a_j for any fixed pair is unchanged, or the array sum parity stays the same. / Conclusion: If target has different parity or inconsistent differences, it is unreachable.
entries.corrected: Invariant: the parity of the array sum. Differences between a chosen and an unchosen element change by 1. Reachability also needs every target entry to be at least its start value and no entry to need more increments than all others combined.

edits.match: Invariant: The difference a_i - a_j for any fixed pair is unchanged, or the array sum parity stays the same.

richText.text: Conclusion: if the target's sum has a different parity from the starting sum, the target is unreachable. Matching parity is necessary but not sufficient: values only grow, so each target entry must be at least its starting value, and no single entry can need more increments than all the other entries combined, because every move increments two distinct entries.

entries.summary: The first Scheduling note shared its title with another note and called its problem "Interval Scheduling with Profits", which is a different problem (weighted interval scheduling needs dynamic programming). It is now titled for the problem it solves and states the unit-length-job assumption the greedy proof relies on.
entries.original: Scheduling — This is often called “Greedy Scheduling with Deadlines” or “Interval Scheduling with Profits.”
entries.corrected: Job Sequencing with Deadlines — unit-length jobs, one slot each; weighted interval scheduling is a different problem.

edits.match: Scheduling
edits.title: Job Sequencing with Deadlines

edits.match: This is often called “Greedy Scheduling with Deadlines” or “Interval Scheduling with Profits.”

richText.text: This problem is usually called job sequencing with deadlines. Each job takes exactly one unit time slot, has a profit, and must finish by its deadline. That unit-length assumption is what makes the greedy below optimal. It is not the same as weighted interval scheduling, where jobs are intervals of different lengths; that problem needs
dynamic programming

entries.summary: The second Scheduling note listed two problems as ones greedy cannot solve, but both examples as stated are classic cases where greedy is optimal: unit-length job sequencing with deadlines, and shortest-processing-time for total completion time on one machine. It also said greedy works whenever optimal substructure holds (it also needs the greedy-choice property) and ended with a broken sentence. The note is renamed and the failing cases now name variants where greedy really fails.
entries.original: General Job Sequencing with Deadlines: picking the highest profit job first might block…; SPT … isn't always optimal; Greedy algorithms work when there are optimal substructure properties.
entries.corrected: Greedy fails for jobs of different lengths with deadlines (weighted on-time jobs) and for weighted completion time without Smith's ratio rule; greedy needs both the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure.

edits.match: Scheduling
edits.title: When Greedy Scheduling Works

edits.match: Not all scheduling problems can be solved using greedy methods. Greedy algorithms work when there are optimal substructure properties.

richText.text: Not all scheduling problems can be solved using greedy methods. A greedy algorithm is correct only when the problem has both the greedy-choice property (some optimal solution starts with the locally best choice) and optimal substructure (what remains is a smaller instance of the same problem).

edits.match: General Job Sequencing with Deadlines: Picking the highest profit job first might block other profitable jobs that could have been scheduled, leading to a lower total profit than an optimal solution (which requires considering all possibilities).

richText.text: Jobs with different processing times and deadlines, maximizing the profit of jobs finished on time: taking the most profitable job first can crowd out several smaller jobs that together earn more. This variant is NP-hard in general and is usually solved with pseudo-polynomial dynamic programming. (With unit-length jobs the greedy in
Job Sequencing with Deadlines
is optimal.)

edits.match: Shortest Processing Time (SPT) for all tasks: If the goal is to minimize total completion time, simply processing shortest jobs first isn't always optimal; it depends on the exact objective and constraints.

richText.text: Weighted completion time: on one machine, shortest processing time first (SPT) is optimal for minimizing the plain sum of completion times, but not when jobs carry different weights; then jobs must be ordered by the ratio of processing time to weight (Smith's rule). SPT also stops being optimal once jobs have release times and cannot be preempted.

edits.match: Scheduling problems leads to canonical greedy algorithms. The proof of the greedy approach to a scheduling problem is outlined in A simple illustrative case is the scheduling problem. The greedy approach picks the task that has the earliest deadline..

richText.text: Scheduling problems lead to canonical greedy algorithms. A simple illustrative case is minimizing the maximum lateness of jobs on one machine: processing jobs in order of earliest deadline is optimal, which an exchange argument proves by swapping any adjacent pair that is out of deadline order without increasing the maximum lateness.
